title: Faxian walks to India
hook: the monk Faxian set out on foot for India to find the rules of discipline (Legge, 1886)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the legend of Kumarajiva's tongue, unburned in the fire. Your line was the tongue remained. Did you check what you passed on? Today the traffic runs the other way: a Chinese monk heads west. Day nine hundred five.

A monk in Chang'an has a problem with the rulebook. The monks' rules of discipline, the Vinaya, have reached China only in pieces. The books he can find are broken and incomplete, and he wants the whole rulebook. He could wait for someone to bring the rest. Instead, he decides to go and get it himself, on foot, across a desert and over the mountains, all the way to India. And he writes it all down. Today, Faxian walks to India.
screen: `THE RULEBOOK IN PIECES.` → `GO AND GET IT.` → `ON FOOT, TO INDIA.`

segments.voice: First, the reason. Faxian's own record, which James Legge put into English, opens with it. Living in Chang'an, he grieved that the books of discipline in China were broken and incomplete, so he and a few companions agreed to travel to India to seek the rules. Not treasure, not fame. The rulebook. Second, the desert. His record describes a sea of sand where there are no birds overhead and no animals below, where you look all around and cannot tell which way to go. The only markers of the road, he writes, are the dry bones of travelers who died there. Third, the mountains. Beyond the desert came high passes, snow in winter and summer, cliffs where the path was cut into the rock and the river ran far below. Along the way companions turned back, fell ill, or stayed behind in monasteries. Faxian kept walking. Fourth, India. He reached the places of the Buddha's life, the holy sites he had only read about, and he settled down to study and copy texts of the discipline, so he could carry them home. Here is what makes his record matter. It isn't a legend told by others. It is a traveler's own account, plain and specific, of what he saw: monasteries, customs, rulers, the state of the holy places. Historians still read it for that reason. And at the center of it is one stubborn decision. He wanted the rules whole. So he walked to India.
screen: `THE RULES IN PIECES.` · `A DESERT MARKED BY BONES.` · `SNOW AND CLIFF PASSES.` · `COPYING TEXTS IN INDIA.` · then, large: `HE WALKED TO INDIA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk a little further today. If you can, get up and walk to the far wall of the room, or out the door, and then a few steps past where you would usually stop. If you can't move right now, trace a route you know well in your mind, and add one more street at the end. Notice the moment you pass your usual turning point. Then, standing or sitting, think of one thing you've been meaning to go and get for yourself, instead of waiting for it to arrive. Rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Faxian. The Chinese monk who crossed desert and mountains on foot to find the complete rules of discipline, and wrote down what he saw. Today's word.
Your line: he walked to India. Today, take one step toward something you've been waiting for someone else to bring you. Day nine hundred five.

howItsDone: Buddhist monks and lay pilgrims still travel to the places of the Buddha's life in India and Nepal, and monastic communities study the Vinaya, the rules of discipline Faxian went to find.

notes: Faxian's record paraphrased from Legge's 1886 translation; not quoted because exact wording was not certain. Legge's text says Fa-hien deplored the 'mutilated and imperfect state' of the Books of Discipline; the desert passage mentions no birds, no animals, and the dry bones of the dead as the only markers. Verify the paraphrase.
Under the claims rule, the year (399) and the number of companions are omitted. The snow "in winter and summer" detail is paraphrased from his description of the mountains; verify.
'Historians still read it for that reason' is a general claim; confirm.

Editor pass: practice rewritten from slow breath-per-step walking (close to day 887's walking practice and the step-breath pacing on days 900 and 902) to literally walking past your usual stopping point; pronunciation changed from vih-NUH-yuh to VIN-uh-yuh.

Audit: hook's "some are garbled, and nobody can say for certain how a monastery should run" was an unsourced overstatement; it now stays with what Faxian's record says (the books were broken and incomplete).
